In typical stars, these reactions take place at very low energy, and many of them have very small rates, making it difficult to measure them directly in the laboratory. On the theoretical side, the low-energy regime is governed by quantum-mechanical phenomena like tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects. This review summarizes the state of the art in the theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and describes new ideas for studying these reactions on Earth.

title: Colloquium: Materials That Exceed Classical Thermodynamic Bounds On Properties
authors: Roderic S. Lakes
abstract:
Author(s): Roderic S. Lakes

Classical thermodynamic bounds provide constraints on values that are expected in measurements of certain physical properties. In a variety of fields, some measurements exceed these bounds. This apparent violation of thermodynamics arises because the measurements are made in ways that violate the underlying assumptions made when deriving these bounds. This Colloquium describes a wide variety of circumstances where such violations occur and which of the underlying assumptions are violated in each case. It also describes how interesting material properties can be developed using materials designed to violate these assumptions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021002] Published Wed May 14, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews materials that appear to violate classical thermodynamic bounds on properties, explaining that the violations arise from violating assumptions in the bounds' derivations.
motivation: To clarify why some measured material properties exceed classical thermodynamic bounds and to show how designing materials to violate these assumptions can lead to interesting properties.
method: The paper is a review (Colloquium) that surveys various circumstances where thermodynamic bounds are exceeded, categorizing the violated assumptions and discussing how materials can be designed accordingly.
result: It identifies multiple cases where measurements exceed bounds due to assumptions like equilibrium, homogeneity, or linearity being violated, and demonstrates how this can be exploited for material design.
conclusion: The apparent violations are not actual violations of thermodynamics but result from misapplying the bounds; understanding this allows for the development of materials with enhanced properties.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: This review summarizes how neutron star observations (gravitational waves and X-ray pulse profiles) constrain the dense matter equation of state, comparing to nuclear theory predictions.
motivation: Understanding the behavior of matter at extreme densities is fundamental to nuclear physics and astrophysics, and neutron stars provide a unique laboratory.
method: The paper reviews recent observational results from binary neutron star mergers (gravitational waves) and X-ray pulse profile measurements, and compares them to theoretical predictions from nuclear equation of state calculations.
result: The measurements constrain neutron star masses, radii, and central densities, providing insights into the equation of state at supranuclear densities.
conclusion: Current observations are consistent with a range of equations of state, and future observations will further refine our understanding.

authors: Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, And Yuanning Gao
abstract:
Author(s): Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, and Yuanning Gao

Hadron spectroscopy is a frontier of particle physics; searching for new hadrons is crucial for validating the theory of strong interaction (QCD). Investigating how charmonium, a bound state of charm and anticharm quarks, decays and searching for new charmoniumlike states yield valuable insights into strong interaction mechanisms, including quark confinement and gluon binding. Hadrons produced at e− collisions decaying to open-charm meson pairs are a primary source of experimental information for these investigations. This Colloquium reviews current progress from BARBAR, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments. As BESIII accumulates high-precision data, it has emerged as the leading facility for measuring hadron production in charm-meson pair systems, and recent advances are highlighted.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021001] Published Fri Apr 03, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews hadron production in open-charm meson pairs at e+e− colliders, focusing on charmonium decays and searches for new charmoniumlike states.
motivation: The paper aims to summarize experimental progress in hadron spectroscopy, which is crucial for validating QCD and understanding strong interaction mechanisms.
method: It reviews results from experiments such as BaBar, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII, highlighting recent advances in measuring hadron production in charm-meson pair systems.
result: The review highlights BESIII's emergence as a leading facility for such measurements and summarizes recent findings in charmonium decays and new charmoniumlike states.
conclusion: The paper concludes that continued high-precision data from BESIII will further advance our understanding of hadron spectroscopy and strong interactions.

title: Colloquium: Planetary Radar At The Arecibo Observatory
authors: Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, And Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín
abstract:
Author(s): Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, and Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín

For more than two decades, the planetary radar installed at the Arecibo Telescope was the most sensitive instrument of its kind, harnessing the penetrating power of radio waves to perform observations of the (sub)surface of planets, moons, and asteroids in the Solar System—providing a unique perspective on those bodies that helped to drive in situ exploration. This Colloquium presents an overview of the scientific legacy of the Arecibo radar system, focusing on the period posterior to the Gregorian Update in the late 1990s until the unexpected demise of the telescope in 2020. After recalling the basics of planetary radar techniques, it reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, our Moon, and the Saturn system, and highlights its essential role in the characterization of a large sample of near-Earth asteroids and comets.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011003] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the scientific legacy of the planetary radar system at the Arecibo Observatory, focusing on its contributions to planetary science.

method: The authors provide a historical overview, describing the radar techniques used and summarizing key observations of various solar system bodies, including Mercury, Venus, Mars, the Moon, and near-Earth asteroids.
result: The paper details the radar system's contributions to characterizing planetary surfaces and near-Earth objects, and its support for in situ missions.
conclusion: The Arecibo radar system had a significant scientific legacy, and its loss is a major setback for planetary radar studies.

abstract:
Author(s): Tapasi Ghosh and Chris Salter

The Arecibo Observatory, inaugurated in 1963 as the world’s largest single-dish radio telescope, remained at the forefront of astronomy and atmospheric science for more than five decades, until its catastrophic collapse in December 2020. This Colloquium focuses on Arecibo’s enduring legacy in radio astronomy, offering a historical perspective that emphasizes how successive major upgrades of the telescope continuously expanded its observational capabilities and scientific impact. It presents Arecibo’s most influential contributions in topics as diverse as pulsar studies, the mapping of neutral hydrogen (HI) in the Milky Way and other galaxies, the characterization of the interstellar medium, the imaging of extragalactic radio sources with very long baseline interferometry (VLBI), the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI), and being a major contributor to the first-ever detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background.

title: Colloquium: The Cosmic Dipole Anomaly
authors: Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, And Subir Sarkar
abstract:
Author(s): Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, and Subir Sarkar

The cosmological principle, which states that the Universe must be statistically isotropic and homogeneous on large scales, is a foundational principle of the standard model of cosmology, known as lambda cold dark matter (ΛCDM). The validity of this principle can be tested by assessing the compatibility of a dipole anisotropy in the large-scale distribution of matter with the dipole observed in the cosmic microwave background, interpreted in the ΛCDM model as due to our local peculiar motion. This Colloquium describes the methodology for such a test and presents its outcome based on the analysis of recent large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars, revealing a significant inconsistency between the two dipoles. The authors review these recent findings, as well as potential biases, systematic issues, and alternate interpretations, and discuss how this anomaly could challenge the standard description of our Universe based on the ΛCDM model.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041001] Published Thu Dec 11, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the cosmic dipole anomaly, a potential violation of the cosmological principle, and its implications for the standard model of cosmology.
motivation: The cosmological principle is foundational to the standard model, and testing it via the dipole anomaly could reveal fundamental issues with our understanding of the universe.
method: The authors review recent analyses of large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars, comparing the dipole in their distribution to the cosmic microwave background dipole, and discuss potential biases and systematic effects.
result: The analyses reveal a significant inconsistency between the matter distribution dipole and the CMB dipole, challenging the standard interpretation.
conclusion: The cosmic dipole anomaly may indicate a breakdown of the cosmological principle, potentially requiring modifications to the standard model of cosmology.

result: The review discusses how self-interactions affect dark matter halos and presents current constraints from galaxy to large-scale structure observations.
conclusion: The paper concludes that self-interacting dark matter remains a viable candidate, with ongoing and future observations expected to provide further tests.

title: Prospects For Supersymmetry At High-Luminosity Lhc
authors: Howard Baer, Vernon Barger, Jessica Bolich, Juhi Dutta, Dakotah Martinez, Shadman Salam, Dibyashree Sengupta, And Kairui Zhang
abstract:
Author(s): Howard Baer, Vernon Barger, Jessica Bolich, Juhi Dutta, Dakotah Martinez, Shadman Salam, Dibyashree Sengupta, and Kairui Zhang

Supersymmetry remains one of the leading candidates for physics beyond the standard model, offering a compelling framework to address the hierarchy of scales. Its theoretical appeal has inspired decades of intensive model building and experimental searches. Recent results have placed stringent bounds on the supersymmetric parameter space, sharpening the focus on the remaining viable models. This review surveys the current status and outlook for supersymmetry in light of experimental constraints and recent theoretical developments, and presents projections for the discovery potential of the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider across multiple search channels and a variety of well-motivated scenarios.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045001] Published Fri Oct 17, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the prospects for supersymmetry at the High-Luminosity LHC, focusing on experimental searches and model constraints.
motivation: Supersymmetry is a leading candidate for physics beyond the Standard Model, and the paper aims to assess its viability given current experimental bounds and future LHC capabilities.
method: The paper is a review that surveys recent experimental constraints and theoretical developments, and presents projections for discovery potential across multiple search channels and scenarios.
result: It provides an overview of the current status of supersymmetry and outlines the expected sensitivity of the HL-LHC to various supersymmetric models.
conclusion: The paper concludes that while supersymmetry remains viable, the HL-LHC will significantly test many models, potentially leading to discovery or further constraints.

title: Nobel Lecture: Physics Is A Point Of View
authors: John J. Hopfield
abstract:
Author(s): John J. Hopfield

The 2024 Nobel Prize for Physics was shared by John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton. This paper is the text of the address given in conjunction with the award.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 030501] Published Mon Aug 25, 2025.
tldr: This is the Nobel Lecture by John Hopfield, reflecting on his scientific journey and the role of physics in understanding complex systems, rather than presenting new research.
motivation: The lecture aims to share personal insights and perspectives on physics, inspired by his Nobel Prize, and to discuss the interdisciplinary nature of his work.
method: The paper is a narrative lecture, not a technical research paper, with no formal methodology.
result: No new experimental or theoretical results are presented; it is a retrospective and philosophical discussion.
conclusion: The lecture emphasizes the importance of physics as a viewpoint for understanding nature, but it does not contribute to the specific research directions listed.

title: Codata Recommended Values Of The Fundamental Physical Constants: 2022
authors: Peter J. Mohr, David B. Newell, Barry N. Taylor, And Eite Tiesinga
abstract:
Author(s): Peter J. Mohr, David B. Newell, Barry N. Taylor, and Eite Tiesinga

This review contains the 2022 self-consistent set of values of the constants and conversion factors of physics and chemistry recommended by the Committee on Data for Science and Technology (CODATA). The CODATA values are based on a least-squares adjustment that takes into account all data available up to the end of 2022. Details of the data selection and methodology are described.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025002] Published Wed Apr 30, 2025.
tldr: This paper provides the 2022 CODATA recommended values of fundamental physical constants, which are essential for metrology but not directly related to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.
motivation: To provide an updated, self-consistent set of fundamental constants for use in physics and chemistry, based on all available data up to 2022.
method: A least-squares adjustment of all relevant experimental and theoretical data, following CODATA's established methodology.
result: A new set of recommended values for fundamental constants and conversion factors, with improved precision and consistency.
conclusion: The CODATA 2022 values serve as the international standard for fundamental constants, but they do not contribute to the specified research directions.
